about.title: Moreno Valley Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: A work injury rarely arrives at a convenient moment. One shift you are lifting, driving, or climbing in Moreno Valley; the next you are juggling medical appointments, missed paychecks, and unfamiliar forms. Under California law, workers' compensation is generally your only claim against your own employer, and it pays regardless of fault. Still, when someone outside your employer contributed to the harm — a subcontractor on a Riverside County job site, a property owner who left a hazard in place, the maker of faulty equipment, or another driver who struck you while you were working — a separate injury claim may be available alongside workers' comp. Work-related driving matters here: Moreno Valley recorded 842 injury collisions in 2025, with 1,239 people hurt, and reported crashes cluster on Fridays between 5 and 7 p.m. along corridors such as SR-60, Perris Boulevard, Heacock Street, and Alessandro Boulevard. LawProactive is free and connects you with an independent attorney who can sort out which path fits your situation.

whyChoose.title: Why Moreno Valley Workers Turn to LawProactive

items.title: Two Claims, Not One
items.desc: Workers' comp is usually the exclusive remedy against your employer, but a negligent subcontractor, property owner, equipment maker, or driver can be pursued separately. The attorney we connect you with looks for both.

items.title: Deadlines Explained Plainly
items.desc: California expects you to report a work injury to your employer within 30 days, and any third-party claim carries a two-year filing window. Knowing which clock applies keeps options open.

items.title: Protection From Pushback
items.desc: Retaliation for reporting a workplace injury is illegal in California. Network attorneys take cases on contingency, so there is no fee unless there is a recovery.

items.question: I was hit on SR-60 while driving for my job in Moreno Valley. Is that a workers' comp case or a car accident case?
items.answer: It can be both. Because you were working, workers' compensation should cover medical care and part of your lost wages regardless of who caused the crash. If another driver was at fault, that driver is a third party, and a separate injury claim may be possible on top of comp. An attorney can review the police report and your employment details to see how the two fit together.

items.question: How quickly do I need to tell my employer about a work injury?
items.answer: California asks you to report the injury to your employer within 30 days. Doing it in writing, even a short email or text, creates a record that helps later. Waiting longer can complicate benefits, so it is better to report early even if the injury seems minor at first.

items.question: Can my employer fire me or cut my hours for filing a claim?
items.answer: No. Retaliating against a worker for reporting an injury or filing for workers' compensation is illegal in California. If you notice demotion, reduced shifts, or termination after you reported, mention it to the attorney you are connected with — it may be a separate issue worth raising.
